exhibits.story:
The suanpan (simplified Chinese: 算盘; traditional Chinese: 算盤; pinyin: suànpán), also spelled suan pan or souanpan) is an abacus of Chinese origin. The earliest known written documentation of the Chinese abacus dates to the 2nd century BCE during the Han dynasty, and it was later described in a 190 CE book of the Eastern Han dynasty, namely Supplementary Notes on the Art of Figures written by Xu Yue. However, the exact design of this suanpan is not known.
Usually, a suanpan is about 20 cm (8 in) tall and it comes in various widths depending on the application.  It usually has more than seven rods.  There are two beads on each rod in the upper deck and five beads on each rod in the bottom deck.  The beads are usually rounded and made of a hardwood.  The beads are counted by moving them up or down towards the beam.  The suanpan can be reset to the starting position instantly by a quick jerk around the horizontal axis to spin all the beads away from the horizontal beam at the center.
Suanpans can be used for functions other than counting.  Unlike the simple counting board used in elementary schools, very efficient suanpan techniques have been developed to do multiplication, division, addition, subtraction, square root and cube root operations at high speed.
The modern suanpan has 4+1 beads, colored beads to indicate position and a clear-all button. When the clear-all button is pressed, two mechanical levers push the top row beads to the top position and the bottom row beads to the bottom position, thus clearing all numbers to zero.  This replaces clearing the beads by hand, or quickly rotating the suanpan around its horizontal center line to clear the beads by centrifugal force.
exhibits.printText: A traditional Chinese counting tool used for mathematical calculations. It uses classic 2:5 and 5:5 bead arrangements, which allow for decimal and hexadecimal calculations. The central panel displays symbols for longevity and prosperity. Think of it as an early calculator; other civilizations used similar tools.

exhibits.title: Foo Dogs
exhibits.subtitle: Shishi
exhibits.printText: Foo dogs originated in China as mythical guardian figures. They are traditionally depicted as stylized lions rather than actual dogs and usually come in male and female pairs. The statues symbolize protection, prosperity, and success. They were designed to keep negative energy or spirits from entering a house or building, similar to gargoyles in Europe.

exhibits.title: Rattan Rickshaw Hat
exhibits.subtitle: Asian Conical Hat
exhibits.printText: This style of hat was invented in China to protect against intense sun and heat. The term “rickshaw” was coined in Japan in the 1860s and spread across much of Asia. The hats are made of split bamboo or rattan woven with palm leaves for ventilation. Today they are rarely used but are celebrated for their intricate craftsmanship.

exhibits.subtitle: Chinese Lunar New Year Decor
exhibits.printText: Chinese Lunar New Year decor is used to sweep out negative energy and invite wealth. This piece displays cranes, which represent longevity, wisdom, peace, and high status. The deer represents wealth and good fortune. When it is given as a gift, the giver is wishing the recipient great abundance.

exhibits.title: Leather Flight Helmet
exhibits.subtitle: English Royal Air Force Flight Helmet
exhibits.printText: This Royal Air Force leather flight helmet is from World War II. The helmet was officially introduced in October 1943. Helmets like this were worn by Spitfire and Hurricane fighter pilots, Lancaster bomber crews, and Fleet Air Arm pilots. Years later, the Triumph Spitfire car was named after the Supermarine Spitfire fighter plane.

exhibits.title: Vintage Hand Carved Wood Maraca
exhibits.subtitle: Maraca (Ceremonial Music)
exhibits.printText: Maracas trace back hundreds of years to the Indigenous Taíno people of the Caribbean. They were originally made from gourds filled with small stones or seeds. During the tourism boom of the 1940s to 1960s, local artisans began carving maracas from dense tropical woods to sell to tourists.

exhibits.title: Necklace
exhibits.subtitle: Lei Hua Necklace
exhibits.printText: This necklace from Hawaii is called a Lei Hua and is made from natural seeds. The necklace serves as symbols of wealth, affection, and social rank. When given it is an offering of affection, good will and aloha. Aloha is a philosophy that represents living in harmony, and having deep connection with others and the environment.

exhibits.title: Ceremonial Tool
exhibits.subtitle: Tumi
exhibits.printText: The tumi is deeply rooted in the pre-Columbian civilizations of Peru. The ornate face represents Naylamp, who, according to legend, grew wings at the end of his life and flew into the sky. Ancient Andean surgeons used specialized sharp tumis to perform cranial trepanation, an early form of brain surgery.

exhibits.title: Honey Locust Tree Seed Pod
exhibits.subtitle: Gleditsia triacanthos
exhibits.printText: This oversized seed pod comes from a tree that coexisted with woolly mammoths, which ate its pods. Historically, Native American tribes used the sweet pulp for food and the wood to make bows. Today, the trees are known for exceptional tolerance of pollution, road salt, and harsh city environments.

exhibits.title: Woolly Mammoth Tooth
exhibits.subtitle: Mammuthus primigenius
exhibits.printText: This molar belonged to a woolly mammoth, a cold-adapted relative of today’s elephants. During the last Ice Age, glaciers held so much water that sea level stood far lower, and the land around Point Pleasant lay miles inland from the coast. It was found in fishing nets off Point Pleasant in the 1980s.
